preamble.summary: LXX 2 Chronicles tracks MT closely. The book's most significant LXX-tradition feature is not a divergence in the standard text but an appendix: the Prayer of Manasseh, a short deuterocanonical composition that expands the brief note at 33:13 about Manasseh's repentance. The Prayer circulated in Greek, was included in some LXX manuscript traditions (especially as part of the 'Odes' collection), and became part of the Eastern Orthodox canon and the Protestant Apocrypha.
preamble.notable_variants: The 'if my people' formula at 7:14 whose Greek vocabulary shapes NT repentance language; the martyrdom of Zechariah at 24:20–22 that Jesus cites at Matthew 23:35 / Luke 11:51 as the boundary-marker of Hebrew Scripture's martyrology; the Prayer of Manasseh tradition growing out of the one-verse note at 33:13; and the Cyrus decree at 36:22–23 that both closes Chronicles (final book of the Hebrew Bible in the Tanakh order) and parallels Ezra 1:1–3 (opening the Persian-period return narrative).
preamble.theological_legacy: 2 Chronicles 24:20–22 is the text behind Jesus' climactic accusation in Matthew 23:35 ('from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berekiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar'). The Jewish canonical order placed 2 Chronicles last, so Abel-to-Zechariah spans the whole canon. LXX-order readers would not have had this effect directly; the accusation only lands with full force against the Hebrew canonical arrangement.

renderings.mt_reading: וְיִכָּנְעוּ עַמִּי אֲשֶׁר נִקְרָא־שְׁמִי עֲלֵיהֶם וְיִתְפַּלְלוּ וִיבַקְשׁוּ פָנַי וְיָשֻׁבוּ מִדַּרְכֵיהֶם הָרָעִים
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐντραπῇ ὁ λαός μου ἐφ᾽ οὓς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐπ᾽ αὐτούς καὶ προσεύξωνται καὶ ζητήσωσιν τὸ πρόσωπόν μου καὶ ἀποστραφῶσιν ἀπὸ τῶν ὁδῶν αὐτῶν τῶν πονηρῶν
renderings.mt_rendering: My people who are called by My Name humble themselves, pray, seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways
renderings.lxx_rendering: And my people on whom my name has been called be turned in shame, and pray and seek my face and turn away from their evil ways
notes: The LXX's four-fold pattern — humble / pray / seek face / turn — is preserved precisely. The verb apostraphōsin ('turn away from') is the standard LXX verb for teshuvah (repentance) and carries into NT usage as metanoeō and epistrophē.

The formula 'my people on whom my name has been called' uses a LXX idiom (epikaleō plus name) that the NT inherits: Acts 15:17 (James's speech at the Jerusalem Council) quotes Amos 9:12 LXX with exactly this 'nations on whom my name has been called' formula.

renderings.mt_reading: וַיִּרְגְּמוּ אֹתוֹ אֶבֶן בְּמִצְוַת הַמֶּלֶךְ בַּחֲצַר בֵּית יְהוָה
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν δι᾽ ἐντολῆς Ιωας τοῦ βασιλέως ἐν αὐλῇ οἴκου κυρίου
renderings.mt_rendering: They conspired against him and stoned him to death at the king's command in the courtyard of the house of the LORD
renderings.lxx_rendering: And they stoned him by the commandment of King Joash in the court of the house of the Lord
notes: Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51 both cite this martyrdom of Zechariah son of Jehoiada (the Chronicler's narrative). Matthew calls him 'Zechariah son of Berekiah,' which is a crux — some scholars think Matthew or a tradition conflates the priest-martyr with Zechariah the prophet (son of Berekiah, Zech 1:1).

In the Hebrew canonical order, 2 Chronicles was the last book of the Writings and hence the last book of Scripture. 'From the blood of Abel (Genesis 4) to the blood of Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24)' meant 'from the first to the last martyr in Scripture.' The LXX canonical order, by contrast, places the Prophets after Chronicles, so the Hebrew-order resonance would have been foreign to Greek-only readers.
This is one of the clearest cases where Jesus' rhetoric assumes the Jewish-Hebrew canonical order, not the LXX order — a data-point in the history of the biblical canon.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ προσηύξατο πρὸς αὐτόν καὶ ἐπήκουσεν αὐτοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: He prayed to him, and God was moved by his plea
renderings.lxx_rendering: And he prayed to him, and he listened to him
notes: The MT note on Manasseh's prayer is brief: 'he prayed … and God was moved.' The absence of any actual prayer text invited early Jewish expansion, and the Prayer of Manasseh — a short (15-verse) Greek composition — circulated as Manasseh's prayer in Hellenistic Jewish piety.

The Prayer of Manasseh appears in the 'Odes' section at the back of many LXX manuscript traditions (together with the Song of the Three, the Song of Moses, the Magnificat, and other canticles). It was included in the Vulgate as an appendix, read liturgically in Eastern Orthodox traditions, and placed in the Protestant Apocrypha.
This is one of the clearest cases of an LXX-manuscript-adjacent composition growing out of a textual gap in MT, filling it with a Hellenistic Jewish devotional supplement.

renderings.mt_reading: כָּל־מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם
renderings.lxx_reading: πάσας τὰς βασιλείας τῆς γῆς ἔδωκέν μοι κύριος ὁ θεὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth
renderings.lxx_rendering: All the kingdoms of the earth the Lord, the God of heaven, has given to me
notes: The closing verse of 2 Chronicles — the Cyrus decree to permit the return from exile — is preserved in the LXX both here and at Ezra 1:1–3. The Greek Bible thus ends the Writings (if 2 Chronicles is last) and begins Ezra with the same Cyrus-decree language.

Matthew 28:18 ('all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me') may intentionally echo the Cyrus decree language — transferred from the Persian king to the risen Christ — with 'heaven and earth' preserving the LXX Chronicler's 'God of heaven … kingdoms of the earth' word-pair.
If the echo is deliberate, the Great Commission is framed as a transcendent Cyrus decree: the true king of the kingdoms of the earth sends his emissaries, now, to all nations.
